text: Before opening SQL Server Management Studio, we sketch the query's logic on paper. What tables it needs, what the output grain is, and the plain-English version of the active and churned rule.

Two decisions matter most before a line of SQL gets written. First, the grain: exactly one row per customer, never one row per order. Get that wrong and joins fan out and silently inflate counts. Second, the reference point for today: one parameterized as-of date, never a hardcoded function buried inside the logic.

The rule gets written in plain English first. Last order date, days since that order, purchases in the trailing twelve months. Then active if under ninety days, churned if over ninety with two or more prior purchases, otherwise not yet retained.

This query does exactly one job, classification. Rates, trends, and region breakdowns are DAX measures and Tableau calculated fields built on top of it later. Keeping the SQL this focused is what keeps it simple enough to verify by hand.
The grain is fixed, the date is parameterized, the logic is written in English. Next: sketching the two dashboard pages themselves, before Power BI opens either.
